title: Palaces of pearls
hook: if I had palaces of pearls and jewels, may I never forget You (Sri Rag M1, ang 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, shabad: a hymn, and the Word itself, sung at every turning of a life. Today, the first hymn of this stretch, and it begins in a dream house.

A real estate app, late at night. Infinity pool. Floor-to-ceiling windows over the ocean. A kitchen bigger than a whole apartment, a garden, room for everyone you love. Guru Nanak built a dream house too, in words. Near the start of the Guru Granth Sahib's main body, in Sri Rag, he raises a palace wall by jeweled wall. And then he asks one question about it.
screen: `A REAL ESTATE APP AT MIDNIGHT.` → `GURU NANAK BUILDS A DREAM HOUSE.` → `THEN ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The shabad is on ang 14. It begins, in effect: if I had a palace built of pearls, inlaid with jewels, its walls plastered with musk and saffron, sandalwood and aloe, a joy to come home to. Then the turn: let it not be that, seeing all this, I go astray, forget You, and Your Name no longer comes to mind. Then the refrain, the rahao, the line tradition treats as the hymn's center: without the Lord my soul burns to ashes; I asked my Guru, and I saw there is no other place. Then he does it again, three more times, each bigger. If the floor were paved with diamonds and rubies, and a beautiful companion waited on a jeweled bed. If I became a siddha, a yogi with miraculous powers, appearing and vanishing at will. If I became a sultan, raising armies, sitting on a throne, giving orders. Each time, the same ending: let me not forget You. Notice what Guru Nanak doesn't say. He doesn't say palaces are evil, or beauty is a trap, or the rich are lost. Sikh teaching doesn't ask people to give up homes, families or work; the Gurus lived as householders. The danger he names is narrower and sharper: forgetting. A beautiful thing can fill the view so completely that the Giver drops out of the picture. The hymn doesn't ask for less. It asks to remember, even with more. And it's set in Sri Rag, a raag tradition associates with evening and seriousness: a grave melody for a dream house.
screen: `A PALACE OF PEARLS AND MUSK.` · `LEST I FORGET YOU.` · `JEWELS, POWERS, A THRONE.` · `NOT RENUNCIATION: REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `MAY I NOT FORGET.`

segments.voice: Build your dream house in your mind, the view, the kitchen, the morning light, whoever you'd want there, and enjoy it for a few breaths; you're allowed. Then ask Guru Nanak's question: in that house, would I still remember what matters most, still call my mother, still notice the person who cleans the pool? Let the house go gently, like setting down a heavy box, and if you pray, say Waheguru as you let go.
Rahao, the refrain, the line tradition treats as a hymn's center: here, after every luxury and power Guru Nanak imagines, it asks only this, that none of it make him forget the One.
Your line: may I not forget. Not less, just remembering. Day six hundred forty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its refrain, that without the Lord the soul burns and there is no other place, is often the line congregations repeat.

what it means: a hymn against forgetting; wealth, beauty and power are dangerous only if they push out the Name.
what a scholar hears: the four-stanza escalation (palace, jeweled bed, siddhi powers, sultanate) uses the rahao as the hymn's thesis, a pattern Guru Nanak uses in other Sri Rag shabads too.

chat.says: Is Guru Nanak's palace-of-pearls hymn saying wealth is bad?
options: No: it asks not to forget the One amid all of it; the danger is forgetting.
Yes, it says a Sikh should give up a beautiful home and live poor.
It says only rulers and yogis forget God; ordinary people are safe.
chat.meaning: Guru Nanak doesn't call palaces evil; the Gurus lived as householders. Each stanza asks the same thing: let none of it make me forget You.

rahao.meaning: the refrain, treated as a hymn's center

Sri Rag.meaning: a raag tradition links with evening and seriousness

siddha.meaning: a yogi said to have miraculous powers

sultan.meaning: a king, a ruler with armies and a throne

sources.ref: Sri Rag M1, Ang 14 (moti ta mandar oosareh)

notes: The shabad is paraphrased; confirm the four stanzas as summarized (palace of pearls with musk, saffron, aloe, sandal; floor of diamonds and rubies with a companion on a jeweled bed; siddhi powers; a sultan with armies and throne) and the rahao 'har bin jeeo jal bal jaao, mai apna gur pooch dekhiaa avar naahee thaao'.
Sri Rag's association with evening and seriousness is traditional; confirm.
'Near the very start of the main body' refers to Sri Rag beginning on ang 14.
